svg.title: Event-Driven Architecture in Microsoft Fabric
svg.desc: An architecture diagram showing streaming sources feeding a Fabric Eventstream, which ingests and optionally transforms events before fanning out to two destinations: an Eventhouse KQL database as the real-time speed layer, and a Lakehouse as the historical batch layer, together forming a lambda-architecture pattern. Eventhouse data also mirrors into OneLake so every Fabric engine can query it without copying. Data Activator monitors Real-Time hub, KQL queries, and Power BI reports and fires actions — notifications, pipeline runs, Spark jobs, Dataflows, User Data Functions, and Power Automate flows — when threshold or pattern conditions are met, contrasted against Data Factory's traditional fixed-schedule execution. A cross-cutting band below the flow covers idempotency and replay: Eventstream's at-least-once delivery means duplicates are possible, so destinations deduplicate using KQL arg_max or Delta MERGE keyed on event ID; a state and windowing panel explains tumbling, hopping, session, and sliding windows; and a batch-vs-stream boundary panel contrasts Direct Ingestion against Event Processing transformation. A legend explains the color coding, and two warning callouts cover Eventhouse's three-stage throttling escalation and the cold-start warm-up latency architects must design around.
svg.text: Eventstream ingests and shapes events, fans out to a real-time speed layer and a historical batch layer, and Activator reacts — with idempotency and replay handled at the edges.

g.title: Streaming sources — Kafka, Kinesis, MQTT, IoT Hub, Pub/Sub, plus Fabric/Azure job and OneLake events themselves, feed directly into Eventstream.

g.text: Direct Ingestion — low latency, low CU
g.title: Fabric Eventstream — a no-code pipeline: sources feed a default stream, which can pass through optional chained transform operators (filter, aggregate, windowed dedupe, routing) before fanning out to one or more destinations.

g.aria-label: Eventhouse KQL database — real-time speed layer
g.title: Eventhouse (KQL database) — organizes ingested records by arrival time for fast indexed queries, and mirrors data to OneLake as a single logical Delta copy for other Fabric engines to read without moving it.
Lakehouse — the same Eventstream simultaneously writes here as the batch layer holding full history, forming a lambda-architecture pattern alongside the Eventhouse speed layer.

svg.text: lambda-architecture pattern: one stream, dual write, two query shapes

g.title: Real-Time hub — the tenant-wide counterpart of OneLake for data in motion: it catalogs eventstreams, KQL database tables, Microsoft source streams, and Fabric/Azure events so Activator and other consumers can discover and react to them in one place.

g.text: contrast: Data Factory runs on a
g.title: Data Activator — a real-time engine that monitors data flowing through Real-Time hub, KQL queries, or Power BI reports and fires automated actions when threshold, pattern, or KQL-defined conditions are met, contrasted with Data Factory's traditional fixed-schedule execution model.
Actions fired — Activator rules trigger notifications (Teams, email), Fabric pipeline or Copy job runs, Spark job or Dataflow executions, User Data Functions, or Power Automate flows.

g.aria-label: Warning: Eventhouse throttling escalates in three stages
g.title: Warning: Eventhouse throttling escalates in three stages when query demand exceeds capacity — proactive (queries slowed, ingestion unaffected), reactive (both paused, no data lost), extreme-reactive (both paused, risk of data loss after a holding period).

Warning: cold-start warm-up latency — an Eventhouse compute node becomes available within 5 to 10 seconds of a cold start; architects should account for this when designing latency-sensitive pipelines with idle periods.

svg.text: Cross-cutting concerns — idempotency, replay, and state
These apply across every lane above, not just at one stage of the flow.

g.text: Eventhouse → KQL arg_max() by event ID
Lakehouse → Delta MERGE keyed on event ID
safe because it is keyed, not additive.
g.title: Idempotency and replay — Eventstream provides at-least-once delivery, so duplicate events are possible; deduplicate at the destination using KQL arg_max() by event ID for Eventhouse or Delta MERGE logic keyed on event ID for Lakehouse.

g.text: State lives in the window buffer while
after landing, organized by arrival time.
g.title: Windowing and state — Eventstream supports four temporal windowing types with distinct semantics: tumbling (non-overlapping fixed intervals), hopping (overlapping fixed intervals), session (dynamic duration based on gaps), and sliding (continuously advancing fixed duration).

g.text: lower latency, lower CU cost. Start
here; push filtering to query time.
Filter close to the source — CU spent
g.title: Batch-vs-stream boundary — Direct Ingestion sends raw events straight to a destination with lower latency and lower CU cost than routing through transformation first; start with Direct Ingestion and only introduce Event Processing when volume reduction, enrichment, or content-based routing is specifically required.
